entries.meaning: To look at something for a period of time, following what happens. ---
examples: I watch the weather report before I leave for work.
We watched the fireworks from the roof.
He has been watching the same show for three hours.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (watch a movie), intransitive (just stand and watch)
entries.contrast: Ends in -ch, so the third person takes -es: watches, never watchs.

entries.meaning: To look at something, especially deliberately or from a particular place. ---
examples: Millions of people view the parade online every year.
We viewed three apartments on Saturday.
The exhibit can be viewed from the balcony.

entries.meaning: To look at something very quickly and then look away. ---
examples: I glance at my phone far too often.
She glanced over her shoulder and kept walking.
He was glancing at the clock every few seconds.
entries.contrast: Almost always needs a preposition: glance at the menu, glance over a letter — not glance the menu.

entries.meaning: To look steadily at something for a long time, often without thinking. ---
examples: Tourists gaze up at the ceiling for a long time.
She gazed out the window and said nothing.
They stood gazing into the fire.
entries.contrast: Needs a preposition: gaze at, gaze into, gaze out of.

entries.meaning: To look hard at something that is difficult to see. ---
examples: I peer at the screen whenever the letters are small.
He peered through the fence to see the dog.
She was peering into the dark hallway.
entries.contrast: Takes at, into or through. The noun peer (ровесник, коллега) is spelled the same but has nothing to do with looking.

entries.meaning: To look at something quickly and secretly, often when you should not. ---
examples: Do not peek while I wrap the gift.
The kids peeked into the box anyway.
She caught me peeking at her notes.
entries.contrast: Peek sounds exactly like peak (вершина) and pique (задеть). Only peek has to do with looking.

entries.meaning: To see something for a very short moment and not clearly. ---
examples: From the train you glimpse the ocean for a second.
I glimpsed her face in the crowd and then lost her.
We had only glimpsed the house from the road.
entries.contrast: The verb takes the object directly (glimpse the ship), but the noun needs of: catch a glimpse of the ship.

entries.meaning: To see something happen, especially a crime or an important event. ---
examples: Hundreds of people witness the ceremony every year.
Two neighbors witnessed the accident.
He has witnessed a lot of change in this town.

entries.meaning: To look at something carefully to check that it is correct or safe. ---
examples: Officials inspect the kitchen twice a year.
He inspected the tires before the long drive.
They are inspecting the roof for storm damage.

entries.meaning: To look over something quickly, usually to find one particular thing. ---
examples: I scan the headlines over breakfast.
She scanned the room for an empty seat.
He was scanning the list for his own name.
entries.contrast: One short vowel plus one final consonant, so the n doubles: scanned, scanning.

entries.meaning: To look over the whole of something in order to judge it. ---
examples: Researchers survey two thousand voters every month.
The pilot surveyed the damage from the air.
They are surveying the land before they build.
entries.contrast: The verb is stressed on the second syllable (sur-VAY); the noun on the first (SUR-vay). Vowel plus y keeps the y: surveys, surveyed.

entries.meaning: To examine something very closely and critically. ---
examples: Auditors scrutinize every receipt.
The judge scrutinized the witness for a long moment.
His record has been scrutinized by the press.
entries.contrast: American spelling is -ize; British writing uses scrutinise.

entries.meaning: To look at someone in a long angry way. ---
examples: Some drivers glare when you take too long.
The teacher glared at the boy in the back row.
She just sat there glaring at her plate.
entries.contrast: The angry sense takes at: glare at someone. The same verb also means to shine painfully: the sun glared off the snow.

entries.meaning: To look with your eyes partly closed because of bright light or poor sight. ---
examples: I squint whenever I forget my glasses.
He squinted at the tiny print on the label.
She was squinting into the afternoon sun.

entries.meaning: To shut and open your eyes quickly, or of a light, to flash on and off. ---
examples: Most people blink about fifteen times a minute.
The light blinked twice and went out.
He stared at me without blinking.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (blink your eyes), intransitive (the light blinked)

entries.meaning: To close and open one eye quickly as a friendly or secret signal. ---
examples: Kids wink when they think they are being funny.
She winked at me across the table.
He kept winking to show that he was joking.
entries.contrast: The person you signal takes at: wink at me, not wink me.

entries.meaning: To look at someone or something with obvious interest or suspicion. ---
examples: Shoppers eye the new phones through the window.
The dog eyed my sandwich the whole time.
He was eyeing the last slice of pizza.
entries.contrast: The -ing form keeps the e: eyeing. (Eying is possible but eyeing is the normal American spelling.)

entries.meaning: To look through things casually, without looking for anything in particular. ---
examples: I browse the shelves whenever I have time.
We browsed the market for an hour.
She was browsing online during the whole meeting.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (browse the catalog), intransitive (we are just browsing)

entries.meaning: To read something quickly to get the main idea. ---
examples: Editors skim the first page before reading closely.
I skimmed the article on the bus.
He was skimming the report, not really reading it.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (skim the article), intransitive (skim through a report)
entries.contrast: The final m doubles: skimmed, skimming.

entries.meaning: To watch something over time to see how it changes. ---
examples: Nurses monitor his heart rate all night.
We monitored the storm on radar.
The site is being monitored for fraud.
entries.contrast: Stress falls on the first syllable, so the r does not double: monitored, monitoring.

entries.meaning: To watch someone secretly, or to catch sight of something suddenly. ---
examples: Neighbors spy on each other in that building.
She spied a familiar face in the crowd.
He was caught spying through the blinds.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (spy a familiar face), intransitive (spy on the neighbors)
entries.contrast: Consonant plus y turns to i: spies, spied; the -ing form keeps the y: spying. Secret watching takes on: spy on someone.

entries.meaning: To make out something that is faint or not obvious. ---
examples: Older readers discern the difference at once.
I discerned a note of doubt in her answer.
A clear pattern could be discerned in the data.

entries.meaning: To find exactly where something or someone is. ---
examples: The app can locate the nearest station for you.
Rescuers located the hikers before dark.
The office is located on the third floor.

entries.meaning: To follow signs or clues back to the source of something. ---
examples: Detectives trace the call to a hotel downtown.
She traced the smell to a burnt wire.
The money has been traced to an offshore account.

entries.meaning: To see something that was being searched for or watched for, usually at a distance. ---
examples: Sailors often sight whales off this coast.
A ranger sighted the missing dog near the river.
Three eagles were sighted here last spring.
entries.contrast: Sight sounds exactly like site (место) and cite (цитировать). Only sight has to do with seeing.

entries.meaning: To notice something consciously, or for a feeling to show on someone's face. ---
examples: Loud noise does not register when you are that tired.
The joke registered a second too late.
I could see the news slowly registering on her face.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (her face registered surprise), intransitive (the name did not register)
entries.contrast: Stress is on the first syllable, so the r does not double: registered, registering.

entries.meaning: To come into sight, or to look a certain way to the people watching. ---
examples: Stars appear as soon as the sky darkens.
A crack appeared in the glass overnight.
He has appeared on that show twice.
entries.contrast: In the meaning to seem, it is followed by an adjective or by to be: she appears tired, it appears to be broken.

entries.meaning: To give the impression of being something. ---
examples: You seem tired today.
It seemed like a good idea at the time.
Nothing has seemed normal since Monday.
entries.contrast: Sounds exactly like seam (шов). Seem is not used in the -ing form: say it seems fine, not it is seeming fine.

entries.meaning: To put something where people can see it. ---
examples: Museums display only part of what they own.
The store displayed the new phones by the door.
The results are displayed on the screen.
entries.contrast: Vowel plus y keeps the y: displays, displayed — not displaid.

entries.meaning: To uncover something, or to let something be reached by light, air or another influence. ---
examples: Photographers expose the film to light for a fraction of a second.
The storm exposed the roots of the old tree.
Children should not be exposed to that much noise.
entries.contrast: What someone is brought into contact with takes to: exposed to sunlight, exposed to the language.

entries.meaning: To keep something from being seen or known. ---
examples: Curtains conceal the wires behind the desk.
He concealed his surprise very well.
The camera was concealed inside a clock.

entries.meaning: To remove a cover, or to find out something that was hidden. ---
examples: Journalists uncover stories that no one wants told.
We uncovered an old wood floor under the carpet.
New evidence has been uncovered this week.

entries.meaning: To make something unclear to see, or to become unclear. ---
examples: Tears blur everything for a minute.
The rain blurred the lights along the road.
The background has been deliberately blurred.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (tears blur your vision), intransitive (the edges blurred)
entries.contrast: One short vowel plus one final consonant, so the r doubles: blurred, blurring.

entries.meaning: To make something look or sound bigger than it really is. ---
examples: These lenses magnify the text four times.
The mirror magnified every flaw.
The sound was magnified by the empty hall.

entries.meaning: To shine suddenly and briefly, or to make a light do that. ---
examples: Warning lights flash when the door is open.
Something flashed in the water near the boat.
The sign has been flashing all night.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (flash a light at someone), intransitive (the sign flashed)

entries.meaning: To shine with an unsteady light that keeps going weak and strong. ---
examples: Old bulbs flicker before they die.
The candle flickered and went out.
The screen kept flickering during the call.

entries.meaning: To shine softly, usually because a surface is clean or smooth. ---
examples: Clean windows gleam in the morning light.
His shoes gleamed under the stage lights.
A knife was gleaming on the counter.

entries.meaning: To give off a steady, soft light without a flame. ---
examples: Embers glow long after the fire dies.
Her face glowed in the candlelight.
The screen was still glowing at midnight.

entries.meaning: To shine with many small quick points of light. ---
examples: Fresh snow sparkles in the sun.
The water sparkled far below us.
Her eyes were sparkling with the news.

entries.meaning: To shine with a hard, bright, broken light. ---
examples: Not everything that glitters is gold.
The dress glittered under the stage lights.
Broken glass was glittering on the pavement.

entries.meaning: To make someone unable to see because of too much light, or to impress them greatly. ---
examples: Bright headlights dazzle oncoming drivers.
The show dazzled the whole crowd.
We were dazzled by the view from the top.

entries.meaning: To light something up so it can be seen. ---
examples: Streetlights illuminate the path at night.
A single lamp illuminated the whole room.
The bridge is illuminated on holidays.
entries.contrast: Double l, single m: illuminate, not iluminate.

entries.meaning: To take away someone's sight, usually for a moment. ---
examples: Snow can blind you on a sunny day.
The flash blinded me for a second.
He was blinded by the low winter sun.

entries.meaning: To give a particular impression when heard. ---
examples: Those two words sound the same to me.
Her voice sounded strange on the phone.
The alarm has been sounding for ten minutes.
entries.русский: звучать, казаться на слух; подавать сигнал
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive (it sounds good), transitive (sound the alarm)
entries.contrast: An adjective follows directly: it sounds good. Before a noun use like: it sounds like a train.

entries.meaning: For a sound to come back off a surface and be heard again. ---
examples: These walls echo every footstep.
His question echoed down the hallway.
The room was echoing with laughter.
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive (the hall echoes), transitive (he echoed her words)
entries.contrast: Ends in -o, so the third person adds -es: echoes, not echos.

entries.meaning: To listen secretly to a conversation that is not meant for you. ---
examples: It is rude to eavesdrop.
She eavesdropped on the call from the hallway.
I caught him eavesdropping outside the door.
entries.contrast: The final p doubles: eavesdropped, eavesdropping. It takes on: eavesdrop on a conversation.

entries.meaning: To make a low continuous humming sound like an insect. ---
examples: Bees buzz around the porch all summer.
My phone buzzed twice during dinner.
The old lights were buzzing overhead.

entries.meaning: To make a low steady sound, or to sing with your lips closed. ---
examples: Refrigerators hum at night when the house is quiet.
He hummed the tune all the way home.
The machine was humming softly in the corner.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (hum a tune), intransitive (the fridge hums)
entries.contrast: The final m doubles: hummed, humming.

entries.meaning: To make the clear ringing sound of a bell. ---
examples: Church bells chime at noon here.
The clock chimed six times.
We could hear bells chiming across the valley.
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive (the clock chimed), transitive (chime the hour)

entries.meaning: To make a long harsh sound, the way old wood or hinges do. ---
examples: Old stairs creak no matter how quietly you walk.
The door creaked open behind me.
The floorboards were creaking upstairs.
entries.contrast: Creak sounds exactly like creek (ручей), but only creak is a sound.

entries.meaning: To make a short high sound, like a mouse or a dry hinge. ---
examples: New shoes squeak on a gym floor.
The gate squeaked when I pushed it.
A mouse was squeaking somewhere behind the wall.

entries.meaning: To make a series of short hard knocking sounds. ---
examples: Loose windows rattle in the wind.
The truck rattled over the old bridge.
Something was rattling around in the trunk.
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive (the window rattles), transitive (rattle the keys)

entries.meaning: To make the soft dry sound of leaves or paper moving. ---
examples: Dry leaves rustle underfoot in October.
Her dress rustled as she stood up.
We heard something rustling in the bushes.
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive (leaves rustle), transitive (rustle the papers)
entries.contrast: The t is silent: RUH-suhl, like castle and whistle.

entries.meaning: To make a loud breaking sound when something hard is crushed or chewed. ---
examples: Fresh snow crunches under your boots.
He crunched an ice cube between his teeth.
The gravel was crunching behind us.
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive (the gravel crunched), transitive (crunch an apple)

entries.meaning: To make the hissing sound of food cooking in hot fat. ---
examples: Onions sizzle the moment they hit the pan.
The steak sizzled on the grill.
Bacon was sizzling when I came downstairs.

entries.meaning: To make a short high electronic sound. ---
examples: The microwave beeps when it is done.
A truck beeped at us on the corner.
My watch kept beeping during the movie.
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive (the timer beeped), transitive (beep the horn)

entries.meaning: To make a very loud deep continuous sound. ---
examples: Jet engines roar on takeoff.
The crowd roared when he finally scored.
Traffic was roaring past the open window.

entries.meaning: To make a high clear sound by blowing air through your lips or a small opening. ---
examples: Some kettles whistle when the water boils.
He whistled for the dog.
She was whistling the same three notes all morning.
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive (he whistled), transitive (whistle a tune)
entries.contrast: The t is silent: WIS-uhl.

entries.meaning: To make a long s sound, like a snake or escaping steam. ---
examples: Cats hiss when they feel cornered.
The radiator hissed all night.
Steam was hissing out of the pipe.

entries.meaning: To make someone unable to hear, usually for a short time. ---
examples: Sirens deafen you at close range.
The explosion deafened the workers nearby.
We were deafened by the music in that club.
entries.contrast: The ea in deaf and deafen is /ɛ/ as in bed, not the /iː/ of leaf.

entries.meaning: To make a sound quieter or less clear by covering it. ---
examples: Thick curtains muffle the street noise.
Snow muffled every sound in the yard.
His voice was muffled by the mask.

entries.meaning: To make a sound or signal louder or stronger. ---
examples: Speakers amplify the sound for the back rows.
The empty hall amplified every footstep.
The signal is being amplified twice along the way.

entries.meaning: To become quiet, or to make someone be quiet. ---
examples: Parents hush their kids when the lights go down.
The crowd hushed as the curtain rose.
She was hushing the baby in the next room.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (hush the baby), intransitive (the room hushed)

entries.meaning: For a sound to go on ringing, or for an idea to strike people as true. ---
examples: Low notes resonate through the floor.
His speech resonated with young voters.
The sound was still resonating in my ears.
entries.contrast: In the figurative sense it takes with: the story resonated with readers.

entries.meaning: To shake with very small fast movements that you can feel or hear. ---
examples: Phones vibrate instead of ringing in meetings.
The whole table vibrated when the train passed.
My phone was vibrating in my pocket.
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive (my phone vibrated), transitive (the motor vibrates the plate)

entries.meaning: To breathe in through the nose in order to smell something. ---
examples: Dogs sniff everything on a walk.
She sniffed the milk before pouring it.
He was sniffing the air as if something were burning.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (sniff the milk), intransitive (the dog sniffed at my shoe)

entries.meaning: To breathe air, smoke or a smell into your lungs. ---
examples: Try not to inhale the dust.
He inhaled deeply and started again.
She had inhaled smoke and needed oxygen.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (inhale the smoke), intransitive (inhale slowly)

entries.meaning: To smell very strongly and unpleasantly. ---
examples: Those old sneakers reek.
The whole room reeked of fish.
His coat was reeking of smoke.
entries.contrast: The source of the smell takes of: it reeks of gas, not it reeks gas.

entries.meaning: To notice something by its smell, or to give something a pleasant smell. ---
examples: Hounds scent a fox from a mile away.
The bear scented us and ran.
These candles are scented with vanilla.
entries.contrast: The c is silent, so scent sounds exactly like sent and cent.

entries.meaning: To notice the flavor of food or drink, or to have a particular flavor. ---
examples: These grapes taste sour.
I tasted the soup and added more salt.
Have you ever tasted real maple syrup?
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive (it tastes sweet), transitive (taste the soup)
entries.contrast: An adjective follows directly: it tastes sweet. Before a noun use like: it tastes like lemon.

entries.meaning: To enjoy a taste or an experience slowly and fully. ---
examples: Slow down and savor the first bite.
She savored every minute of the trip.
He sat there savoring his coffee.
entries.contrast: American spelling is savor; British writing uses savour.

entries.meaning: To try a small amount of something in order to judge it. ---
examples: Shoppers sample the cheese at the counter.
We sampled four kinds of local honey.
He was sampling everything on the table.

entries.meaning: To move your tongue over something. ---
examples: Dogs lick your hand to say hello.
The cat licked the plate clean.
She was licking the spoon when I walked in.

entries.meaning: To eat something in small bites. ---
examples: Mice nibble the corners of the box.
He nibbled a cracker and pushed the plate away.
She was nibbling on a carrot the whole time.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (nibble a cracker), intransitive (nibble on a carrot)
entries.contrast: Eating slowly takes on or at: nibble on a cookie, nibble at her lunch.

entries.meaning: To drink something slowly in very small amounts. ---
examples: Kids sip their drinks through straws.
She sipped her tea and said nothing.
He was sipping something hot from a paper cup.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (sip her tea), intransitive (sip at a glass)
entries.contrast: The final p doubles: sipped, sipping.

entries.meaning: To give food or drink a particular taste. ---
examples: Fresh herbs flavor the whole dish.
She flavored the cream with vanilla.
The rice was flavored with saffron.
entries.contrast: American spelling is flavor; British writing uses flavour.

entries.meaning: To add salt, pepper or spices to food to improve its taste. ---
examples: Good cooks season the meat before it goes in the pan.
I seasoned the soup a little too heavily.
The chicken had been seasoned overnight.

entries.meaning: To push steadily on something with your hand or body. ---
examples: Press the button twice to start the machine.
He pressed his hand flat against the cold glass.
She was pressing the fabric down with both palms.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (press the button), intransitive (press against the door)

entries.meaning: To move your hand or a cloth back and forth over a surface with pressure. ---
examples: I rub my eyes whenever I am tired.
He rubbed the stain with a wet cloth.
She was rubbing her sore shoulder.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (rub your eyes), intransitive (the shoe rubs)
entries.contrast: The final b doubles: rubbed, rubbing.

entries.meaning: To touch something lightly in passing. ---
examples: Low branches brush the roof of the bus.
Her sleeve brushed my arm as she passed.
Something soft was brushing against my leg.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (brush your coat), intransitive (brush against the wall)
entries.contrast: A light accidental touch takes against: his coat brushed against mine.

entries.meaning: To move your hand gently and repeatedly over a surface. ---
examples: Some cats let strangers stroke them.
She stroked the dog behind the ears.
He sat stroking his beard while he thought.

entries.meaning: To touch something lightly several times with a flat hand. ---
examples: Coaches pat players on the back after a game.
He patted the seat next to him.
She was patting the dough into shape.
entries.contrast: The final t doubles: patted, patting.

entries.meaning: To hit something quickly and lightly, usually more than once. ---
examples: I tap the screen twice to zoom in.
Someone tapped me on the shoulder.
He kept tapping his pen against the desk.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (tap the screen), intransitive (tap on the glass)
entries.contrast: The final p doubles: tapped, tapping. To touch a person it takes on: tap him on the arm.

entries.meaning: To push a finger or a pointed object quickly into something. ---
examples: Do not poke the fire with your hand.
She poked the cake to see if it was done.
The kids were poking each other under the table.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (poke the cake), intransitive (poke at the fire)

entries.meaning: To push someone or something gently, often to get attention. ---
examples: Friends nudge you when you have said too much.
She nudged me and pointed at the door.
He was nudging the box across the floor with his foot.

entries.meaning: To squeeze something tightly between a finger and a thumb, or between two hard surfaces. ---
examples: New shoes always pinch at first.
He pinched my arm to wake me up.
The strap was pinching her shoulder.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (pinch my arm), intransitive (these shoes pinch)

entries.meaning: To press something firmly from two sides. ---
examples: Squeeze the lemon over the fish before serving.
She squeezed my hand and smiled.
He was squeezing the last of the toothpaste out.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (squeeze the lemon), intransitive (squeeze through a gap)

entries.meaning: To hold something tightly so it cannot slip. ---
examples: Good tires grip the road even in rain.
He gripped the rail with both hands.
She was gripping the steering wheel far too tightly.
entries.contrast: The final p doubles: gripped, gripping.

entries.meaning: To hold something very tightly, often out of fear or need. ---
examples: Passengers clutch their bags on the subway.
She clutched the letter to her chest.
He was clutching a coffee in one hand and his keys in the other.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (clutch a bag), intransitive (clutch at a branch)
entries.contrast: A desperate grab takes at: clutch at the rail.

entries.meaning: To touch or hold something with your hands. ---
examples: Please handle the glasses carefully.
He handled the vase as if it were made of paper.
These boxes have been handled roughly.
entries.русский: трогать руками, брать в руки; обращаться с

entries.meaning: To touch someone lightly so that they laugh or twitch, or to cause a light itchy feeling. ---
examples: Wool sweaters tickle my neck.
He tickled the baby until she laughed.
My throat has been tickling all morning.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (tickle the baby), intransitive (this sweater tickles)

entries.meaning: To feel an uncomfortable sensation on the skin that makes you want to scratch. ---
examples: Mosquito bites itch for days.
My eyes itched all through the spring.
The wool was itching against my skin.
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive (my arm itches), transitive (the wool itches me)

entries.meaning: To rub the skin with your nails, or to make a thin mark on a surface. ---
examples: Cats scratch the furniture when they are bored.
He scratched his head and said nothing.
She had scratched the side of the car backing out.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (scratch your arm), intransitive (the dog scratched at the door)

entries.meaning: To touch or scrape a surface lightly while passing it. ---
examples: Low branches graze the roof of the bus.
The ball grazed his helmet and went wide.
She had grazed her knee on the pavement.
entries.contrast: The same verb also means to eat grass: cows graze in the field.

entries.meaning: To feel around for something clumsily, usually because you cannot see. ---
examples: Cold fingers fumble with small buttons.
He fumbled for the light switch in the dark.
She was fumbling with her keys at the door.
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive (fumble for the switch), transitive (he fumbled the ball)
entries.contrast: Searching by touch takes for or with: fumble for the switch, fumble with a zipper.

entries.meaning: To feel a light prickling sensation on the skin. ---
examples: Cold air makes your cheeks tingle.
My fingers tingled after the snowball fight.
Her whole arm was tingling by then.

entries.meaning: To feel a steady dull pain. ---
examples: My knees ache before it rains.
His back ached after the long drive.
She has been aching all over since the game.
entries.contrast: The ch is pronounced /k/: AYK, not like church.

entries.meaning: To take away feeling from a part of the body. ---
examples: Cold water will numb the pain for a while.
The dentist numbed the whole side of my mouth.
My feet were numbed by the cold.
entries.contrast: The b is silent: NUM.

entries.meaning: To explore something by touch or by careful questioning.
examples: Doctors probe the wound for fragments.
Investigators probed the company's records for a year.
The whole area is being probed for leaks.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (probe the wound), intransitive (probe into his past)
